analysis.one_liner: Taxes large corporations 95% on profits above their pre-pandemic average through 2026.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2024, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never advanced; it died when the Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new federal tax on "excess profits": if a large corporation (with at least $500 million in annual gross receipts) earned more than its inflation-adjusted average profit from 2015 through 2019, it would pay a 95% tax on the excess, capped at 75% of its modified taxable income, for tax years through 2026. It would also disallow several deductions large corporations currently use and expand the limits on deductible executive pay. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday taxpayers would benefit from the revenue the new tax would raise, since a 95% tax on corporate profits above pre-2020 levels would shift a portion of those windfalls back to the public instead of leaving them for shareholders and buybacks. It would also apply to foreign corporations' U.S.-connected income, closing a route that currently escapes the tax. Small and mid-sized businesses with under $500 million in receipts would be exempt entirely.

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a 95% tax on corporate profits above each company's inflation-adjusted 2015-2019 average, recovering revenue from large corporations whose profits surged above their historical levels.

It narrows tax breaks those corporations currently use, including the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income and preferential depreciation rules, so their taxable income is measured more fully.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations — roughly the biggest U.S. companies with $500 million or more in gross receipts — would pay the new tax on profits above their 2015-2019 average, and their shareholders would bear it through lower returns. Some cost could also pass to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Profits above a 2015-2019 baseline can reflect legitimate growth or investment, not price gouging; the tax cannot distinguish between the two, and a 95% rate on that excess could discourage companies from expanding output or reporting income during the covered years.

The tax applies to all large C corporations with $500 million in receipts, not only those accused of price gouging, and the benchmark years (2015-2019) are fixed, so fast-growing firms in new industries would owe the tax even without raising prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would claw back a large share of profits that big corporations earn above their pre-2020 levels, money that could otherwise go to shareholders or buybacks, and it broadens the tax base by denying several deductions. The strongest good-faith objection is that a 95% rate above a historical baseline is extremely steep: it could discourage expansion, and companies that legitimately grew because of real demand or innovation would pay as heavily as price-gougers, since the tax cannot tell the two apart. The cap at 75% of income and the 2026 sunset soften the stakes somewhat. Whether it is good policy depends heavily on how one weighs redistribution against those investment effects.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never advanced past its initial referral to the Senate Finance Committee, so it died without a vote when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sanders and Markey introduced S. 4642 on July 9, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the bill sat in committee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the remainder of the 118th Congress.
The bill had one cosponsor, Sen. Markey, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations, whose windfall profits above pre-2020 levels remain untaxed by any federal excess-profits tax, are better off because the bill never advanced; no comparable tax was enacted in its place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations avoiding the excess-profits tax

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Corporate Greed Act to impose a 95% excess-profits tax on large corporations through 2026.

for.name: Sen. Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: The committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — which ended the bill's only path forward.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; it was sponsored by an independent senator with a single Democratic cosponsor.

industries.industry: Large C corporations with $500M+ in gross receipts
industries.note: They would owe a 95% surtax on profits above their pre-2020 inflation-adjusted average and would lose several deductions, sharply raising their tax bills while the tax is in effect.
Less profit flowing to shareholders and buybacks, and expanded executive pay rules; the bill's revenue would come out of returns to concentrated wealth.
